methods.label: Follow every displayed arrow and add path counts
methods.explanation:
The direction rule applies to every arrowhead shown, including the small solid ones. These solid arrows point rightward along their segments; the three hollow arrows on the middle horizontal line point leftward.

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_12B_Q22_question_fig1.svg)

At the right endpoint of each hollow arrow, all three incident arrows point away from that vertex. The bug cannot reach such a vertex from \(A\). At the left endpoint, all three incident arrows point into the vertex, so a bug arriving there cannot continue to \(B\). Consequently no successful path uses a middle horizontal segment or any of its endpoints.

Removing those unusable middle vertices separates successful paths into two cases: paths above \(AB\) and paths below \(AB\). We can count the upper case by writing the number of paths reaching the right endpoint of each horizontal segment. At a merge, add the incoming counts: the possible final incoming segments are different, so these cases do not overlap. At a split, carry the current count to each available continuation.

There are seven successive columns of horizontal segments above \(AB\). Listing the counts from top to bottom within each column gives
\[
(1),\quad(1),\quad(1,1),\quad(1,2),
\]
\[
(3,2),\quad(5),\quad(5).
\]
Here the lower entry in the fourth column is \(1+1=2\). In the fifth column, the upper entry is \(1+2=3\), while the lower entry carries forward \(2\). These merge in the sixth column to give \(3+2=5\), and the final column carries those five paths to \(B\).

The lower half has the same branching and merging pattern, so it also contributes five paths. Every successful path belongs to exactly one of these two cases. Moreover, every usable move goes strictly rightward, so none can repeat a segment. Thus the displayed conditions give
\[
5+5=\boxed{10}
\]
paths. This is absent from the choices and conflicts with the supplied key \(\text{E}:2400\).
